board_events.text: Blow the atom up to the size of a cricket stadium and the nucleus is one grain of rice on the centre pitch.
Nucleons = the particles of the nucleus. Protons carry positive charge; neutrons carry none.
Z = proton number = atomic number. Change Z and you have changed the element itself.
N = neutron number. A = Z + N = mass number = total nucleon count.
About 99.9% of the atom's mass sits inside about one part in a thousand million million of its volume.
Enormous emptiness wrapped around a dense core: the master picture of nuclear physics.

segments.text: <curious>Let me start with one picture, because it will carry you through this entire chapter. Think of an atom as a vast, almost completely empty stadium.

Here is that comparison drawn out. The faint sphere on the left is the electron cloud, and the electrons are just a few spectators wandering the highest, farthest seats. Down at the very centre of the pitch sits a tiny, impossibly dense pebble. That pebble is the nucleus.

The scale is genuinely startling. Blow the whole atom up until it is the size of a cricket stadium, and the nucleus would be about the size of a single grain of rice sitting on the centre pitch. Everything else, all of that space, is empty.

So what is that pebble made of? Two kinds of particle, and collectively we call them nucleons. Protons, which carry positive charge, and neutrons, which are electrically neutral. That is the entire cast of characters.

The proton count earns its own name, the atomic number Z, and it is the fingerprint of the chemical element. Change Z, even by one, and you have not merely modified an element. You have literally turned it into a different element.

The neutron count is N. Add the two together and you get the mass number A, which is just the total number of nucleons packed into the nucleus. A equals Z plus N. Three symbols, and between them they run this entire chapter.

<whisper>Now here is the fact that makes the nucleus so strange. Almost the entire mass of the atom is crammed into that pebble, even though it occupies a laughably small fraction of the atom's volume.

Hold on to this image, because every single result ahead of us grows out of it. Enormous emptiness wrapped around a dense core. Nuclear radius, nuclear density, binding energy, all of it is this one picture written in algebra.
<curious>चलिए एक picture से शुरू करते हैं, क्योंकि यही आपको पूरे chapter में साथ ले जाएगी। Atom को सोचिए एक बहुत बड़े, लगभग पूरी तरह खाली stadium की तरह।

यह रहा वही comparison। बाईं तरफ की faint sphere है electron cloud, और electrons बस कुछ spectators हैं जो सबसे ऊपर वाली, सबसे दूर की seats पर घूम रहे हैं। और pitch के बिल्कुल बीच में बैठा है एक tiny, बेहद dense pebble। वही है nucleus।
Scale सच में चौंका देने वाला है। अगर पूरे atom को बढ़ाकर एक cricket stadium जितना कर दें, तो nucleus होगा centre pitch पर रखे चावल के एक दाने जितना। बाकी सब खाली।
तो यह pebble बना किससे है? दो तरह के particles से, और इन्हें मिलाकर हम कहते हैं nucleons। Protons, जिन पर positive charge है, और neutrons, जो electrically neutral हैं। बस यही पूरा cast है।
Proton count को अपना नाम मिलता है, atomic number Z, और यही chemical element का fingerprint है। Z को एक से भी बदल दीजिए, तो आपने element को modify नहीं किया। आपने उसे सचमुच दूसरा element बना दिया।
Neutron count है N। दोनों को जोड़ दीजिए तो मिलता है mass number A, यानी nucleus में भरे हुए nucleons की कुल संख्या। A बराबर Z plus N। तीन symbols, और यही तीनों पूरा chapter चलाते हैं।
<whisper>अब वो fact जो nucleus को इतना strange बनाता है। Atom का लगभग पूरा mass उसी pebble में ठुँसा हुआ है, जबकि वो atom के volume का हास्यास्पद रूप से छोटा हिस्सा घेरता है।

इस image को पकड़े रखिए, क्योंकि आगे का हर result इसी से निकलता है। बहुत सारा खालीपन, और बीच में एक dense core। Nuclear radius, nuclear density, binding energy, सब कुछ यही picture है algebra में लिखी हुई।

board_events.text: A nuclide is written with the mass number A above and the atomic number Z below the chemical symbol.
Top number A = total nucleons. Bottom number Z = protons.
Uranium-238: Z = 92 protons, A = 238 nucleons, so N = 238 - 92 = 146 neutrons.
The bottom number is redundant with the element name, which is why it is often dropped: carbon-12 is unambiguous.
Every conservation check in this chapter is just: top numbers balance, bottom numbers balance.

segments.text: Every nuclide in this chapter arrives wearing the same uniform, so let us learn to read it in one glance rather than decoding it every time.
Here is the notation unpacked. The chemical symbol sits in the middle. The number written above and to the left is the mass number A. The number written below and to the left is the atomic number Z.

So the top number is the total nucleon count, protons and neutrons together, and the bottom number is the proton count on its own. Two numbers, and they are not independent of each other in what they tell you.

Because the moment you know both, the neutron number falls straight out. N equals A minus Z. Take the total, subtract the protons, and whatever remains has to be neutrons. There is nothing else in there.

Let us run it on uranium. The bottom number is ninety two, so there are ninety two protons. The top number is two hundred and thirty eight, so there are two hundred and thirty eight nucleons in total.
Subtract, and you get one hundred and forty six neutrons. That is the entire composition of the nucleus, read off two small numbers in about three seconds.

You will often see the bottom number left off entirely, written simply as carbon dash twelve or uranium dash two three eight. That is not sloppiness. The element name already fixes Z, so the bottom number is genuinely redundant information.

<whisper>And here is a habit worth building now. Every decay equation you meet later gets checked the same way: top numbers must balance across the arrow, bottom numbers must balance across the arrow. That single check catches most errors.
इस chapter में हर nuclide एक ही uniform पहनकर आता है, तो चलिए इसे एक नज़र में पढ़ना सीख लेते हैं, हर बार decode करने के बजाय।
यह रहा notation खुला हुआ। बीच में chemical symbol है। ऊपर बाईं तरफ लिखा number है mass number A। नीचे बाईं तरफ लिखा number है atomic number Z।
तो ऊपर वाला number है total nucleon count, protons और neutrons दोनों मिलाकर, और नीचे वाला number है सिर्फ proton count। दो numbers, और जो वो बताते हैं उसमें वो एक दूसरे से जुड़े हुए हैं।
क्योंकि जैसे ही आपको दोनों पता हैं, neutron number अपने आप निकल आता है। N बराबर A minus Z। Total लीजिए, protons घटा दीजिए, और जो बचा वो neutrons ही होंगे। अंदर और कुछ है ही नहीं।
चलिए uranium पर चलाते हैं। नीचे वाला number है बानवे, तो बानवे protons हैं। ऊपर वाला है दो सौ अड़तीस, यानी कुल दो सौ अड़तीस nucleons।
घटाइए, और मिलते हैं एक सौ छियालीस neutrons। यही nucleus का पूरा composition है, दो छोटे numbers से लगभग तीन seconds में पढ़ा हुआ।

आप अक्सर देखेंगे कि नीचे वाला number लिखा ही नहीं जाता, बस carbon dash twelve या uranium dash two three eight। यह लापरवाही नहीं है। Element का नाम पहले ही Z fix कर देता है, तो नीचे वाला number सचमुच redundant है।

<whisper>और एक habit अभी से बना लीजिए। आगे आने वाला हर decay equation इसी तरह check होता है: arrow के दोनों तरफ ऊपर वाले numbers बराबर, और नीचे वाले numbers बराबर। यही एक check ज़्यादातर mistakes पकड़ लेता है।

board_events.text: Railway picture: every coach takes up the same fixed length of track, however long the train.
Each nucleon claims the same fixed parcel of space, so adding nucleons simply swells the nucleus.
Volume grows in proportion to A. Radius is the cube root of volume, so radius grows as the cube root of A.
Radius does NOT grow in proportion to A. Cube-root the A-ratio, always.
Limits: this treats the nucleus as a uniform sphere with a sharp edge. Real nuclei have fuzzy surfaces and some are rugby-ball shaped.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a question worth sitting with. If you double the number of nucleons in a nucleus, what happens to its radius? The instinct says double. The instinct is wrong.

Look at what actually happens. Going from A equals eight to A equals sixty four is eight times the nucleons, but the radius only doubles. The packing inside, you will notice, looks identical in all three.

Think about a railway platform where every coach is identical in size, no matter how long the train. One coach takes up a fixed length of track. A ten coach train is twice as long as a five coach train, along that one dimension.

The nucleus behaves astonishingly like that, except in three dimensions. Each nucleon claims the same fixed little parcel of space. So as you add nucleons, the nucleus simply swells to make room, and the matter inside stays packed at exactly the same crushing density.

Now follow the geometry. If every nucleon takes the same volume, then the total volume grows in direct proportion to A. But radius is not volume. Radius is the cube root of volume. So radius grows as the cube root of A.

That gives us the relation you will use in almost every numerical of this subtopic. R equals R nought times A to the power one third, where R nought is about one point two femtometres, fixed by experiment.
<whisper>And the cube root is where the marks are lost. Students see a mass number ratio and write the radius ratio straight down. Always cube-root the A ratio first.

One honest caveat before we move on. This formula treats the nucleus as a uniformly dense sphere with a sharp edge. Real nuclei have fuzzy surfaces and some are rugby-ball shaped, and R nought itself drifts between about one point one and one point three femtometres depending on how you measure radius. It is an excellent trend tool, not a microscopically exact one.
<curious>यह सवाल थोड़ा रुककर सोचने लायक है। अगर nucleus में nucleons की संख्या double कर दें, तो radius का क्या होगा? Instinct कहता है double। और instinct गलत है।
देखिए असल में होता क्या है। A बराबर आठ से A बराबर चौंसठ तक जाने में nucleons आठ गुना हुए, लेकिन radius सिर्फ double हुआ। और ध्यान दीजिए, अंदर की packing तीनों में एक जैसी दिख रही है।

सोचिए एक railway platform, जहाँ हर coach का size एक जैसा है, train चाहे कितनी भी लंबी हो। एक coach track की एक fixed लंबाई लेता है। दस coach की train पाँच coach वाली से दोगुनी लंबी होती है, उस एक dimension में।

Nucleus हैरान करने वाले तरीके से ऐसा ही behave करता है, बस तीन dimensions में। हर nucleon उतनी ही fixed जगह माँगता है। तो जैसे-जैसे nucleons बढ़ते हैं, nucleus बस फैल जाता है, और अंदर का matter उसी crushing density पर packed रहता है।

अब geometry को follow कीजिए। अगर हर nucleon बराबर volume लेता है, तो total volume सीधे A के proportion में बढ़ेगा। लेकिन radius volume नहीं है। Radius है volume का cube root। इसलिए radius बढ़ता है A के cube root की तरह।
इससे मिलता है वो relation जो इस subtopic के लगभग हर numerical में लगेगा। R बराबर R nought into A की power one third, जहाँ R nought लगभग one point two femtometre है, experiment से तय।
<whisper>और marks जाते हैं इसी cube root पर। Students mass number ratio देखते हैं और radius ratio सीधे लिख देते हैं। हमेशा पहले A ratio का cube root लीजिए।

आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक ईमानदार caveat। यह formula nucleus को एक uniformly dense sphere मानता है, sharp edge के साथ। असली nuclei की surfaces fuzzy होती हैं, कुछ rugby ball जैसी shape की होती हैं, और R nought खुद one point one से one point three femtometre के बीच बदलता है, इस पर कि radius नापा कैसे गया। यह trend के लिए बढ़िया tool है, microscopically exact नहीं।

board_events.text: Weigh a nucleus precisely and it comes out lighter than Z separate protons plus N separate neutrons.
The shortfall is called the mass defect. Mass has genuinely gone missing.
The missing mass was converted into the energy that glues the nucleons together.
Mass and energy are two currencies for one quantity, exchangeable at the fixed rate of c squared.
Consequence: 'mass is conserved' is only an excellent approximation. It fails once energies get large, which is exactly where nuclear physics lives.

segments.text: We have accepted that all that mass is locked inside a tiny core. Now a much deeper surprise appears, and it is the surprise the rest of this chapter is built on.

Look at the two bars. The top bar is the total mass of the separate protons and neutrons, weighed individually before you assemble anything. The bottom bar is the mass of the finished nucleus. The bottom bar is shorter.

That is not a measurement error. Weigh a nucleus on a hyper-precise scale and it genuinely comes out lighter than the sum of the loose protons and neutrons that make it up. Some mass is simply not there any more.
We give the shortfall a name, the mass defect. And a name is not an explanation, so the obvious question is the right one to ask. Where did the mass go?

Einstein's relation answers it. Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. Mass and energy are not two separate things that happen to be related. They are two currencies for the same underlying quantity.

So the missing mass was not destroyed. It was converted, and it came out as the energy that glues the nucleons together in the first place. Assembling the nucleus released it; the nucleus is lighter by exactly that amount.

<excited>And the exchange rate is fixed. Not negotiable, not approximate, the same everywhere in the universe: the speed of light squared. That is what makes such a whisper of missing mass worth such an enormous amount of energy.

One consequence is worth stating plainly, because it quietly overturns something you were taught earlier. The statement that mass is conserved is only an excellent approximation. It fails the moment energies become large, and large energies are exactly the regime nuclear physics lives in.
हमने मान लिया कि इतना सारा mass एक tiny core में बंद है। अब एक और गहरी surprise आती है, और बाकी पूरा chapter इसी surprise पर खड़ा है।
दोनों bars देखिए। ऊपर वाला bar है अलग-अलग protons और neutrons का total mass, assemble करने से पहले अलग-अलग तौला हुआ। नीचे वाला bar है तैयार nucleus का mass। नीचे वाला छोटा है।
यह measurement error नहीं है। Nucleus को बेहद precise scale पर तौलिए और वो सचमुच उन loose protons और neutrons के sum से हल्का निकलता है। कुछ mass बस वहाँ है ही नहीं।
इस कमी को हम नाम देते हैं, mass defect। लेकिन नाम explanation नहीं होता, तो सही सवाल वही है जो सामने खड़ा है। वो mass गया कहाँ?
Einstein का relation इसका जवाब देता है। Energy बराबर mass into speed of light का square। Mass और energy दो अलग चीज़ें नहीं हैं जो संयोग से जुड़ी हों। वो एक ही quantity की दो currencies हैं।
तो गायब mass नष्ट नहीं हुआ। वो convert हुआ, और बाहर आया उसी energy के रूप में जो nucleons को आपस में चिपकाती है। Nucleus बनने पर वो energy निकल गई, और nucleus ठीक उतना ही हल्का रह गया।
<excited>और exchange rate fixed है। न negotiable, न approximate, पूरे universe में एक जैसा: speed of light का square। यही वजह है कि इतने से गायब mass की कीमत इतनी भारी energy होती है।

एक नतीजा साफ़ कह देना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि यह चुपचाप पहले पढ़ी हुई एक बात को पलट देता है। यह कहना कि mass conserved होता है, सिर्फ एक बहुत अच्छा approximation है। जैसे ही energies बड़ी होती हैं यह टूट जाता है, और बड़ी energies ही nuclear physics का घर हैं।

board_events.text: Isotopes: same Z, different A. Same element, different mass. Example: hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2, hydrogen-3.
Isobars: same A, different Z. Example: hydrogen-3 and helium-3, both with A = 3.
Isotones: same N, different Z. Example: hydrogen-3 and helium-4, both with N = 2.
Isotones are the only family where you must compute N = A - Z before you can compare.
Anchor each family to its constant: isotopes hold Z, isobars hold A, isotones hold N.
Mnemonic from the chapter: 'Proton, A-equals-bar, Neutron.'

segments.text: Three words that get blurred together in exams more than almost anything else in this chapter. Isotopes, isobars, isotones. Each one holds exactly one quantity fixed, and that is the whole distinction.
Here they are side by side. Notice that in each panel one number is locked and the other is free. Find the locked number and you have named the family.
Isotopes hold Z fixed. Same proton count, different mass number. Hydrogen has three of them: ordinary hydrogen, deuterium, tritium. All hydrogen, because Z stays at one, but their masses climb.

Isobars hold A fixed. Same total nucleon count, different proton count. Hydrogen-three and helium-three both carry three nucleons in total, but one has a single proton and the other has two. Different elements, same weight.

Isotones hold N fixed. Same neutron count, different everything else. Hydrogen-three and helium-four look nothing alike, but hydrogen-three has three minus one, which is two neutrons, and helium-four has four minus two, which is also two neutrons.

<whisper>And that is precisely where isotones catch people out. Isotopes and isobars you can spot by staring at the symbol. Isotones you cannot. You have to subtract first, every time, before you compare anything.
So anchor each family to its constant and the confusion disappears. Isotopes hold the proton number. Isobars hold the mass number. Isotones hold the neutron number.
The chapter gives you a mnemonic for the order, and it is worth memorising cold: Proton, A-equals-bar, Neutron. Isotope, isobar, isotone. Say it once before a paper and it stays put.
तीन शब्द जो exams में इस chapter की लगभग किसी भी और चीज़ से ज़्यादा आपस में गड्डमड्ड होते हैं। Isotopes, isobars, isotones। हर एक ठीक एक quantity को fixed रखता है, और बस यही पूरा फर्क है।
यह रहे तीनों साथ-साथ। ध्यान दीजिए हर panel में एक number locked है और दूसरा free। Locked number ढूँढ लीजिए, family का नाम मिल गया।
Isotopes Z को fixed रखते हैं। Proton count वही, mass number अलग। Hydrogen के तीन हैं: ordinary hydrogen, deuterium, tritium। सब hydrogen हैं, क्योंकि Z एक ही रहता है, पर mass बढ़ता जाता है।

Isobars A को fixed रखते हैं। Total nucleon count वही, proton count अलग। Hydrogen-three और helium-three दोनों में कुल तीन nucleons हैं, पर एक में एक proton है और दूसरे में दो। अलग elements, वही weight।

Isotones N को fixed रखते हैं। Neutron count वही, बाकी सब अलग। Hydrogen-three और helium-four देखने में बिल्कुल अलग हैं, पर hydrogen-three में तीन minus एक यानी दो neutrons हैं, और helium-four में चार minus दो, यानी दो ही neutrons।
<whisper>और isotones यहीं लोगों को फँसाते हैं। Isotopes और isobars आप symbol देखकर पहचान लेंगे। Isotones नहीं। पहले घटाना पड़ेगा, हर बार, तभी compare कर पाएँगे।
तो हर family को उसके constant से बाँध दीजिए, confusion खत्म। Isotopes proton number पकड़ते हैं। Isobars mass number। Isotones neutron number।
Chapter एक mnemonic भी देता है और यह रटने लायक है: Proton, A-equals-bar, Neutron। Isotope, isobar, isotone। Paper से पहले एक बार बोल दीजिए, टिका रहेगा।

board_events.text: Physical input: electron-scattering experiments show nucleons are packed at essentially constant density throughout the interior.
Step 1. Treat the nucleus as a sphere of radius R.
Step 2. Impose the experimental fact that volume scales with nucleon count.
Step 3. The constant four-thirds pi carries no A, so the proportionality passes straight to R cubed.

segments.text: This is a standard board derivation, so let us walk it exactly as an examiner wants to see it. Four steps, and each one has a reason attached, because marks are given for the reasons and not just the algebra.
Here is the whole chain laid out. Notice that it starts with an experimental fact, not with a formula. That is the correct direction, and it is worth saying out loud in your answer.

The physical input comes from electron-scattering experiments. You fire high energy electrons at nuclei and read how they bounce off. What those experiments reveal is that nucleons are packed at essentially constant density right through the nuclear interior.
So step one is pure geometry. Treat the nucleus as a sphere of radius R. Nothing physical yet, just a shape we can compute with.
Its volume is four-thirds pi R cubed. That is the geometry half of the argument, and on its own it tells us nothing about nuclei.

Step two is where the physics enters. Constant density means equal volume per nucleon, so the volume of the nucleus must be directly proportional to the number of nucleons it contains. We impose that on the geometry.
Writing it out, four-thirds pi R cubed is proportional to A. Say why you are allowed to do this: because each nucleon demands the same fixed parcel of space, so the geometry has to obey the physics.
Step three is the algebraic move that does all the work. The constant four-thirds pi does not depend on A at all, so it simply passes straight through the proportionality untouched.

What that leaves is R cubed proportional to A. Take the cube root of both sides and R is proportional to A to the power one third. And notice what that cube root really is. It is not algebraic decoration. It is the geometric signature of incompressible, uniformly packed nuclear matter.

<excited>Step four introduces the proportionality constant, fixed by experiment, and the derivation is finished. R equals R nought A to the one third, with R nought about one point two femtometres. Four steps, each with its reason, and that is exactly the answer an examiner is looking for.
यह एक standard board derivation है, तो चलिए इसे ठीक वैसे चलते हैं जैसे examiner देखना चाहता है। चार steps, और हर step के साथ एक reason, क्योंकि marks reasons पर मिलते हैं, सिर्फ algebra पर नहीं।
यह रही पूरी chain। ध्यान दीजिए यह एक experimental fact से शुरू होती है, formula से नहीं। यही सही direction है, और answer में यह लिखकर बोलना चाहिए।

Physical input आता है electron-scattering experiments से। High energy electrons nuclei पर मारिए और देखिए वो कैसे bounce होते हैं। यही experiments बताते हैं कि nucleons पूरे nuclear interior में लगभग constant density पर packed हैं।
तो step one पूरी तरह geometry है। Nucleus को radius R की एक sphere मान लीजिए। अभी कुछ physical नहीं, बस एक shape जिस पर हिसाब हो सके।
उसका volume है four-thirds pi R cubed। यह argument का geometry वाला हिस्सा है, और अकेले यह nuclei के बारे में कुछ नहीं बताता।

Step two में physics घुसती है। Constant density का मतलब है per nucleon बराबर volume, तो nucleus का volume उसमें मौजूद nucleons की संख्या के सीधे proportion में होना चाहिए। यही हम geometry पर लागू करते हैं।
लिखिए तो, four-thirds pi R cubed proportional to A। और यह भी लिखिए कि ऐसा करने की इजाज़त क्यों है: क्योंकि हर nucleon उतनी ही fixed जगह माँगता है, तो geometry को physics माननी ही पड़ेगी।
Step three वो algebraic move है जो सारा काम करता है। Constant four-thirds pi में A है ही नहीं, तो वो proportionality में से सीधा बाहर निकल जाता है।

बचता है R cubed proportional to A। दोनों तरफ cube root लीजिए और R हो जाता है proportional to A की power one third। और देखिए वो cube root असल में है क्या। यह algebra की सजावट नहीं है। यह incompressible, uniformly packed nuclear matter का geometric signature है।

<excited>Step four में experiment से तय हुआ proportionality constant आता है, और derivation पूरी। R बराबर R nought A to the one third, R nought लगभग one point two femtometre। चार steps, हर एक अपने reason के साथ, और examiner को यही answer चाहिए।

board_events.text: Step 1. Mass of the nucleus is approximately A times the mean nucleon mass.
Step 2. Volume, from the previous derivation, carries a factor of A as well.
Step 3. Form the density and watch A cancel between numerator and denominator.
No A survives on the right, so hydrogen and uranium share one density. About ten to the fourteen times water.

segments.text: This derivation is short, but the chapter calls its result the conceptual heart of the whole subtopic, and I agree. It is also the single most tested trap in this section.
Watch what happens in the fraction. An A appears on top, an A appears on the bottom, and they annihilate each other. Everything left over is a constant.
Step one. The mass of the nucleus is approximately A times m sub N, where m sub N is the mean mass of one nucleon. More nucleons, more mass, in direct proportion.

Step two. The volume comes straight from the derivation we just finished. Substituting R equals R nought A to the one third into four-thirds pi R cubed, the cube undoes the cube root and leaves a clean factor of A.
So the volume is four-thirds pi R nought cubed times A. That factor of A is the entire point. Volume also grows in direct proportion to the nucleon count.
Step three. Now form the density, mass over volume. The numerator carries an A. The denominator carries an A. Cancel them.

What survives is m sub N divided by four-thirds pi R nought cubed. Look at that right-hand side carefully. There is no A anywhere in it. Nothing about how big the nucleus is has survived the cancellation.
Put the numbers in and it comes to about two point three times ten to the seventeen kilograms per cubic metre. Every nucleus, from hydrogen to uranium, carries that same density.

<whisper>Which means a density ratio question between two nuclei has the answer one to one, and you should be writing it down before you have finished reading the question. That figure, incidentally, is roughly ten to the fourteen times the density of water.
यह derivation छोटी है, पर chapter इसके result को पूरे subtopic का conceptual heart कहता है, और मैं सहमत हूँ। यही इस section का सबसे ज़्यादा पूछा जाने वाला trap भी है।
देखिए fraction में होता क्या है। ऊपर एक A आता है, नीचे एक A आता है, और दोनों एक दूसरे को खत्म कर देते हैं। जो बचता है वो एक constant है।
Step one। Nucleus का mass लगभग A into m sub N है, जहाँ m sub N एक nucleon का mean mass है। ज़्यादा nucleons, ज़्यादा mass, सीधे proportion में।
Step two। Volume सीधे उसी derivation से आता है जो अभी पूरी की। R बराबर R nought A to the one third को four-thirds pi R cubed में रखिए, cube उस cube root को खत्म कर देता है और साफ़ A बचता है।
तो volume है four-thirds pi R nought cubed into A। यही A वाला factor पूरी बात है। Volume भी nucleon count के सीधे proportion में बढ़ता है।
Step three। अब density बनाइए, mass बटा volume। ऊपर A है। नीचे A है। दोनों cancel।
बचता है m sub N बटा four-thirds pi R nought cubed। इस right hand side को ध्यान से देखिए। इसमें A कहीं नहीं है। Nucleus कितना बड़ा है, इसका कोई निशान cancellation के बाद बचा ही नहीं।
Numbers रखिए तो यह आता है लगभग two point three into ten to the seventeen kilogram per cubic metre। Hydrogen से uranium तक, हर nucleus की यही density।

<whisper>यानी दो nuclei के बीच density ratio का जवाब है one to one, और वो आपको question पढ़कर खत्म करने से पहले ही लिख देना चाहिए। और वैसे, यह figure पानी की density से लगभग ten to the fourteen गुना है।

board_events.text: Nuclear size and density: the working set
Nuclide notation: mass number A above, atomic number Z below the symbol, with N = A - Z.
R = nuclear radius in metres; A = mass number, dimensionless; R-nought = empirical constant. SI unit of R is the metre, dimensional formula $[M^0 L^1 T^0]$.
The natural unit here is the femtometre, also called the fermi, where $1\ \text{fm} = 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$.
Mean nucleon mass $m_N \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg. SI unit of density kg per cubic metre, dimensional formula $[M^1 L^{-3} T^0]$.
Radius ratio = cube root of the A-ratio. Density ratio = 1 to 1. Always.

segments.text: Let me consolidate the size half of this subtopic into the handful of lines you actually write in an exam. Everything here has been derived; this is the working set.
First, the notation itself, because a question often hides its data inside a symbol. Mass number on top, atomic number below, and the neutron number is the difference between them.
The radius relation. R equals R nought times A to the power one third, with R nought approximately one point two femtometres, which is one point two times ten to the minus fifteen metres.

Know what each symbol is. R is the nuclear radius in metres. A is the mass number and it is dimensionless, just a count. R nought is an empirical constant. The dimensional formula of R is M to the zero, L to the one, T to the zero, which is simply a length.

The natural unit at this scale is the femtometre, also called the fermi, equal to ten to the minus fifteen metres. Nuclear radii come out as a few femtometres, so if your answer is in nanometres you have made a power-of-ten slip.

Now density. Mass over volume, with the nuclear mass written as A times the mean nucleon mass and the volume written as four-thirds pi R nought cubed times A. The A cancels, and you are left with a pure constant of about two point three times ten to the seventeen kilograms per cubic metre.

The mean nucleon mass in there is about one point six six times ten to the minus twenty seven kilograms. The SI unit of density is kilograms per cubic metre, and its dimensional formula is M to the one, L to the minus three, T to the zero.
<whisper>And the one line to carry into the exam hall. Radius ratio means cube-root the A ratio. Density ratio means one to one, no calculation, no exceptions.
चलिए इस subtopic के size वाले हिस्से को उन कुछ lines में समेट देते हैं जो आप exam में सचमुच लिखते हैं। यहाँ सब कुछ derive किया जा चुका है; यह working set है।
पहले notation, क्योंकि question अक्सर अपना data symbol के अंदर छिपा देता है। ऊपर mass number, नीचे atomic number, और neutron number दोनों का अंतर।
अब radius relation। R बराबर R nought into A की power one third, R nought लगभग one point two femtometre, यानी one point two into ten to the minus fifteen metre।

हर symbol पहचानिए। R है nuclear radius, metre में। A है mass number और यह dimensionless है, बस एक count। R nought एक empirical constant है। R का dimensional formula है M to the zero, L to the one, T to the zero, यानी सिर्फ एक length।

इस scale की natural unit है femtometre, जिसे fermi भी कहते हैं, बराबर ten to the minus fifteen metre। Nuclear radii कुछ femtometres में आते हैं, तो अगर आपका answer nanometre में आ रहा है तो power of ten की चूक हुई है।

अब density। Mass बटा volume, जहाँ nuclear mass है A into mean nucleon mass और volume है four-thirds pi R nought cubed into A। A cancel हो जाता है, और बचता है एक pure constant, लगभग two point three into ten to the seventeen kilogram per cubic metre।

उसमें mean nucleon mass है लगभग one point six six into ten to the minus twenty seven kilogram। Density की SI unit है kilogram per cubic metre, और dimensional formula है M to the one, L to the minus three, T to the zero।
<whisper>और exam hall में ले जाने वाली एक line। Radius ratio यानी A ratio का cube root। Density ratio यानी one to one, कोई calculation नहीं, कोई अपवाद नहीं।

sections.title: Formula sheet: the atomic mass unit and the mass-energy bridge

board_events.text: Converting mass into energy: the bridge and the shortcut
The atomic mass unit is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Dimensional formula of mass: $[M^1 L^0 T^0]$.
E in joules, m in kilograms, $c = 3 \times 10^{8}$ m per second. Dimensional formula of energy: $[M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]$.
Procedure: (1) find the missing mass in u; (2) multiply by 931.5 to get MeV; (3) for joules, use $1\ \text{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}$ J.
Never re-derive through E = mc squared in joules under exam pressure. Use the one-line bridge and multiply.

segments.text: Now the energy half of the toolkit. Nuclear masses are tiny and nuclear energies are large, so this section is really about choosing units that keep the arithmetic humane.

The atomic mass unit is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-twelve atom, and that works out to one point six six zero five three nine times ten to the minus twenty seven kilograms. It is a mass, so its dimensional formula is just M to the one.

Why define it that way? Because on this scale a proton weighs almost exactly one unit, a neutron almost exactly one unit, and a nucleus of mass number A weighs almost exactly A units. The numbers stay near one instead of near ten to the minus twenty seven.

The bridge itself. E equals m c squared, and pre-evaluated for one atomic mass unit, one u corresponds to nine hundred and thirty one point five mega electron volts. That second form is what you will actually use.

In the first form, E is in joules, m is in kilograms and c is three times ten to the eight metres per second. Worth checking the dimensions once: mass times velocity squared gives M L squared T to the minus two, which is energy. Good.

These four masses are worth memorising, because problems hand them to you inconsistently. Proton one point zero zero seven two seven six. Neutron one point zero zero eight six six five. Electron zero point zero zero zero five four nine. And the neutral hydrogen atom, one point zero zero seven eight two five, which is the proton plus its electron.

The procedure is three steps. Compute the missing mass in atomic mass units. Multiply by nine hundred and thirty one point five to get mega electron volts. And if the question demands joules, convert with one mega electron volt equals one point six times ten to the minus thirteen joules.

<whisper>Here is the pro-tip the chapter gives, and it saves real minutes. Never re-derive through E equals m c squared in joules under exam pressure. The bridge is that relation already evaluated for you. Memorise it and multiply.
अब toolkit का energy वाला हिस्सा। Nuclear masses बहुत छोटे हैं और nuclear energies बड़ी, तो असल में यह section units चुनने के बारे में है ताकि arithmetic इंसानी बनी रहे।

Atomic mass unit को define किया जाता है carbon-twelve atom के mass के बारहवें हिस्से के रूप में, और वो निकलता है one point six six zero five three nine into ten to the minus twenty seven kilogram। यह mass है, तो dimensional formula बस M to the one।

ऐसे define क्यों किया? क्योंकि इस scale पर proton का weight लगभग ठीक एक unit है, neutron का लगभग ठीक एक unit, और mass number A वाले nucleus का लगभग ठीक A units। Numbers एक के आसपास रहते हैं, ten to the minus twenty seven के आसपास नहीं।
अब bridge। E बराबर m c squared, और एक atomic mass unit के लिए pre-evaluated: one u बराबर nine hundred thirty one point five mega electron volts। असल में आप यही दूसरा form इस्तेमाल करेंगे।

पहले form में E joules में है, m kilograms में और c है three into ten to the eight metre per second। Dimensions एक बार check कर लीजिए: mass into velocity squared देता है M L squared T to the minus two, यानी energy। सही।

ये चार masses याद रखने लायक हैं, क्योंकि questions इन्हें अलग-अलग तरीके से देते हैं। Proton one point zero zero seven two seven six। Neutron one point zero zero eight six six five। Electron zero point zero zero zero five four nine। और neutral hydrogen atom, one point zero zero seven eight two five, जो proton plus उसका electron है।

Procedure तीन steps का है। Missing mass atomic mass units में निकालिए। Nine hundred thirty one point five से multiply कीजिए, mega electron volts मिल गए। और अगर question joules माँगे, तो one mega electron volt बराबर one point six into ten to the minus thirteen joule से convert कीजिए।

<whisper>यह रहा chapter का pro-tip, और यह सचमुच मिनट बचाता है। Exam के दबाव में E बराबर m c squared से joules में दोबारा मत निकालिए। Bridge वही relation है, पहले से हल किया हुआ। याद रखिए और multiply कर दीजिए।

board_events.text: Given: A = 27 and R-nought = 1.2 fm. Required: the nuclear radius R.
The cube root of 27 is exactly 3, so this needs no calculator.
Answer: R is about 3.6 fm.
Examiners choose mass numbers like 8, 27, 64, 125 and 216 precisely so the cube root is instant.

segments.text: A clean board-level question to start with, and the point of it is not the arithmetic. It is the habit of identifying which relation the question is testing before you write anything.
Before we calculate, look at the ladder on the board, because it tells you what kind of number to expect. Aluminium sits at mass number twenty seven, which is a perfect cube.
Write down what you are given. The mass number A is twenty seven. The constant R nought is one point two femtometres. And what is required is the nuclear radius R.
The relation connecting those three is the radius formula. R equals R nought times A to the power one third. That is the whole physics content of this problem.
Now substitute. The cube root of twenty seven is exactly three, because three cubed is twenty seven. No calculator, no approximation, just recognition.
So R equals one point two times three, which is three point six femtometres. In metres, that is three point six times ten to the minus fifteen.
Our answer, then, is a radius of about three point six femtometres. Sanity check the order of magnitude: nuclear radii should land in the range of a few femtometres, and it has.

<whisper>And notice what just happened. A perfect cube under the root kept the arithmetic clean, and that was not an accident. Examiners love mass numbers like eight, twenty seven, sixty four, one hundred and twenty five and two hundred and sixteen for exactly this reason. Learn to spot them.
शुरुआत के लिए एक साफ़-सुथरा board level question, और इसका मकसद arithmetic नहीं है। मकसद है यह आदत कि कुछ लिखने से पहले पहचानिए question कौन सा relation test कर रहा है।
Calculate करने से पहले board पर बनी ladder देखिए, क्योंकि वो बता देती है कि कैसा number आने वाला है। Aluminium का mass number सत्ताईस है, जो एक perfect cube है।
जो दिया है वो लिख लीजिए। Mass number A है सत्ताईस। Constant R nought है one point two femtometre। और चाहिए nuclear radius R।
इन तीनों को जोड़ने वाला relation है radius formula। R बराबर R nought into A की power one third। इस problem में physics बस इतनी ही है।
अब substitute कीजिए। सत्ताईस का cube root ठीक तीन है, क्योंकि तीन का cube सत्ताईस होता है। न calculator, न approximation, बस पहचान।
तो R बराबर one point two into three, यानी three point six femtometre। Metre में यह हुआ three point six into ten to the minus fifteen।
तो हमारा answer है radius लगभग three point six femtometre। Order of magnitude जाँच लीजिए: nuclear radii कुछ femtometres में आने चाहिए, और आए।

<whisper>और ध्यान दीजिए अभी क्या हुआ। Root के नीचे perfect cube होने से arithmetic साफ़ रह गई, और यह इत्तेफ़ाक नहीं था। Examiners आठ, सत्ताईस, चौंसठ, एक सौ पच्चीस और दो सौ सोलह जैसे mass numbers इसी वजह से चुनते हैं। इन्हें पहचानना सीखिए।

board_events.text: The trap: writing the radii as 1 to 27, and the densities as 27 to 1.
Part (a). Radii follow the cube root of the A-ratio, never the A-ratio itself.
Part (b). Nuclear density carries no A at all, so the two densities are simply equal.
Radius questions: cube-root the A-ratio. Density questions: answer 'equal' before you pick up the pen.

segments.text: <curious>This is a classic speed trap, and I want you to notice the trap before we solve it, because recognising the shape of a trap is worth more than solving one instance of it.
Two nuclei, mass numbers in the ratio one to twenty seven. The picture shows what that actually looks like: one nucleus with twenty seven times the nucleons of the other.

Here is what a hurried student writes. Radius ratio one to twenty seven, because the mass numbers were one to twenty seven. And density ratio twenty seven to one, because surely the bigger nucleus is denser. Both of those are wrong.
Take part a properly. Radius does not follow A. Radius follows A to the power one third. So the ratio of radii is the ratio of mass numbers, raised to the power one third.
One over twenty seven, all to the power one third, is one over three. So the radii are in the ratio one to three. Twenty seven times the nucleons, but only three times the radius.
Part b is even shorter, provided you remember the derivation. Nuclear density came out as a constant with no A in it anywhere. The size of the nucleus never entered the final expression.
So the densities are in the ratio one to one. They are equal, and they are equal for any pair of nuclei you could have been given, not just this one.

<whisper>Carry these two reflexes into the hall. If the question says radius, cube-root the A ratio. If the question says density, the answer is equal, and you should be writing it before you have finished reading the question.
<curious>यह एक classic speed trap है, और मैं चाहता हूँ कि हल करने से पहले आप trap को पहचान लें, क्योंकि trap की shape पहचानना उसका एक example हल करने से ज़्यादा कीमती है।
दो nuclei, mass numbers का ratio one to twenty seven। Picture दिखाती है यह असल में कैसा दिखता है: एक nucleus जिसमें दूसरे से सत्ताईस गुना nucleons हैं।

जल्दबाज़ी में student क्या लिखता है, सुनिए। Radius ratio one to twenty seven, क्योंकि mass numbers one to twenty seven थे। और density ratio twenty seven to one, क्योंकि बड़ा nucleus तो ज़्यादा dense होगा ही। दोनों गलत हैं।
Part a ठीक से लीजिए। Radius A को follow नहीं करता। Radius follow करता है A की power one third को। तो radii का ratio है mass numbers का ratio, power one third पर उठाया हुआ।
One बटा twenty seven, पूरे की power one third, बराबर one बटा three। तो radii का ratio है one to three। सत्ताईस गुना nucleons, पर radius सिर्फ तीन गुना।
Part b तो और भी छोटा है, बशर्ते derivation याद हो। Nuclear density एक constant निकली थी जिसमें A कहीं था ही नहीं। Nucleus का size final expression में घुसा ही नहीं।
तो densities का ratio है one to one। बराबर हैं, और किसी भी nuclei की जोड़ी के लिए बराबर होतीं, सिर्फ इसी के लिए नहीं।
<whisper>ये दो reflexes hall में साथ ले जाइए। Question में radius है, तो A ratio का cube root। Question में density है, तो answer है बराबर, और वो question पढ़कर खत्म करने से पहले लिख देना चाहिए।

board_events.text: Part (a). The radius relation is unchanged; only A is large now.
Since 6.2 cubed is about 238.3, take the cube root of 238 as roughly 6.2.
Part (b). Use the bridge, one atomic mass unit to 931.5 MeV, then convert.
Cross-check: $m = 238.05 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \approx 3.95 \times 10^{-25}$ kg, and $mc^2 \approx 3.6 \times 10^{-8}$ J. Agrees.

segments.text: This one deliberately stitches the two halves of the subtopic together, nuclear size and mass-energy equivalence, in a single question. That combination is a JEE Main favourite.
And it has a feature worth noticing on the board: two independent roads to the same energy, which is what lets us check ourselves at the end.
Part a first. The relation has not changed just because uranium is heavy. R equals R nought times A to the one third, with A now two hundred and thirty eight.
Substituting, R equals one point two times the cube root of two hundred and thirty eight femtometres. This time the cube root is not exact, so we estimate it.
Here is the trick. Six point two cubed is about two hundred and thirty eight point three, comfortably close. So the cube root of two hundred and thirty eight is roughly six point two.

That gives R equals one point two times six point two, which is seven point four four, so about seven point four femtometres. Compare that with aluminium's three point six. Nearly nine times the nucleons, but only about twice the radius. The cube root at work again.
Part b. The rest mass is two hundred and thirty eight point zero five atomic mass units, and the bridge says every unit is worth nine hundred and thirty one point five mega electron volts.

Multiply the two together and you get about two point two two times ten to the five mega electron volts. Pause on how large that is: the rest mass of a single uranium nucleus is worth over two hundred thousand mega electron volts.

If the question demands joules, convert with one mega electron volt equals one point six times ten to the minus thirteen joules. That gives about three point five five times ten to the minus eight joules.

<excited>And now the cross-check, which is the real lesson here. Go the long way instead: convert the mass to kilograms, about three point nine five times ten to the minus twenty five, and multiply by c squared, nine times ten to the sixteen. You get three point six times ten to the minus eight joules. The two roads agree, because nine hundred and thirty one point five per unit is nothing but E equals m c squared, pre-evaluated.
यह question जानबूझकर subtopic के दोनों हिस्सों को जोड़ता है, nuclear size और mass-energy equivalence, एक ही सवाल में। यह combination J E E Main का पसंदीदा है।
और board पर एक बात ध्यान देने लायक है: एक ही energy तक पहुँचने के दो अलग रास्ते, जिनसे हम आखिर में खुद को check कर पाएँगे।
पहले part a। Uranium भारी है इससे relation नहीं बदल जाता। R बराबर R nought into A की power one third, और अब A है दो सौ अड़तीस।
Substitute कीजिए, R बराबर one point two into दो सौ अड़तीस का cube root, femtometre में। इस बार cube root exact नहीं है, तो estimate करेंगे।
Trick यह है। Six point two का cube लगभग दो सौ अड़तीस point three होता है, काफी पास। तो दो सौ अड़तीस का cube root लगभग six point two।

इससे R बराबर one point two into six point two, यानी seven point four four, लगभग seven point four femtometre। इसकी तुलना aluminium के three point six से कीजिए। लगभग नौ गुना nucleons, पर radius सिर्फ करीब दोगुना। फिर वही cube root।
अब part b। Rest mass है दो सौ अड़तीस point zero five atomic mass units, और bridge कहता है हर unit की कीमत nine hundred thirty one point five mega electron volts है।

दोनों को multiply कीजिए, मिलता है लगभग two point two two into ten to the five mega electron volts। ज़रा सोचिए यह कितना बड़ा है: एक अकेले uranium nucleus के rest mass की कीमत दो लाख से ज़्यादा mega electron volts।
अगर question joules माँगे, तो one mega electron volt बराबर one point six into ten to the minus thirteen joule से convert कीजिए। तो आता है लगभग three point five five into ten to the minus eight joule।

<excited>और अब cross-check, जो यहाँ की असली सीख है। लंबा रास्ता लीजिए: mass को kilogram में बदलिए, लगभग three point nine five into ten to the minus twenty five, और c squared से multiply कीजिए, nine into ten to the sixteen। मिलता है three point six into ten to the minus eight joule। दोनों रास्ते मिल गए, क्योंकि per unit nine hundred thirty one point five कुछ और नहीं, E बराबर m c squared ही है, पहले से हल किया हुआ।

board_events.text: Given: one solar mass = $2 \times 10^{30}$ kg, nuclear density $\rho = 2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg per cubic metre.
Method 1: straight from the density.
Method 2: treat it literally as a nucleus and count the nucleons.
Answer: R is about 15 km, remarkably close to real neutron stars. Both methods agree because they are the same physical statement seen twice.

segments.text: <excited>This is the question that shows you why this subtopic matters, because we are about to size an astronomical object using nothing but a formula for nuclear radius.

The model is the whole idea. A neutron star is what happens when gravity crushes matter until it reaches the density of a nucleus, so we treat the entire star as a single enormous nucleus of closely packed nucleons.

We are given one solar mass as two times ten to the thirty kilograms, and nuclear density as two point three times ten to the seventeen kilograms per cubic metre. Notice the density is just the number we derived earlier. Nothing new has been supplied.
Method one goes straight through the density, and it does not even mention nuclei. It is pure mass over volume reasoning.

The star's mass is one point five times two times ten to the thirty, which is three times ten to the thirty kilograms. Divide by the density and you get the volume, about one point three times ten to the thirteen cubic metres.

Now invert the sphere formula. R cubed equals three V over four pi, which is about three point one one times ten to the twelve. Take the cube root and R comes out at about one point four six times ten to the four metres, that is fourteen point six kilometres.

Method two is the elegant cross-check, and it treats the star literally as a nucleus. Divide the total mass by the mass of one nucleon and you get the nucleon count, about one point eight one times ten to the fifty seven.
Then apply the nuclear radius formula with that count in place of A. R nought times that number to the power one third gives one point four six times ten to the four metres. Identical.

So the answer is a radius of about fifteen kilometres, which is remarkably close to the radii of real neutron stars. And the two methods had to agree, because treating it as one big nucleus and using the constant nuclear density are the same physical statement viewed two ways.
<excited>यह वो question है जो दिखाता है कि यह subtopic क्यों मायने रखता है, क्योंकि हम एक astronomical object का size निकालने जा रहे हैं, सिर्फ nuclear radius के formula से।
Model ही पूरी बात है। Neutron star वो है जो तब बनता है जब gravity matter को कुचलकर nucleus की density तक ले आती है, तो हम पूरे star को एक विशाल nucleus मान लेते हैं, closely packed nucleons का।

हमें दिया है एक solar mass बराबर two into ten to the thirty kilogram, और nuclear density two point three into ten to the seventeen kilogram per cubic metre। ध्यान दीजिए density वही number है जो हमने पहले derive किया था। नया कुछ नहीं दिया गया।
Method one सीधे density से जाता है, और उसमें nuclei का ज़िक्र तक नहीं आता। बस mass बटा volume की सोच।

Star का mass है one point five into two into ten to the thirty, यानी three into ten to the thirty kilogram। Density से भाग दीजिए तो volume मिलता है, लगभग one point three into ten to the thirteen cubic metre।

अब sphere का formula उलटिए। R cubed बराबर three V बटा four pi, यानी लगभग three point one one into ten to the twelve। Cube root लीजिए और R आता है लगभग one point four six into ten to the four metre, यानी fourteen point six kilometre।

Method two elegant cross-check है, और यह star को सचमुच एक nucleus मानता है। Total mass को एक nucleon के mass से भाग दीजिए तो nucleon count मिलता है, लगभग one point eight one into ten to the fifty seven।
अब उसी count को A की जगह रखकर nuclear radius formula लगाइए। R nought into उस number की power one third देता है one point four six into ten to the four metre। बिल्कुल वही।

तो answer है radius लगभग पंद्रह kilometre, जो असली neutron stars के radii के हैरान करने वाले तरीके से पास है। और दोनों methods को मिलना ही था, क्योंकि इसे एक बड़ा nucleus मानना और constant nuclear density लगाना, एक ही physical statement के दो रूप हैं।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: composition, size and mass-energy

board_events.text: Four pitfalls that cost real marks
1. Forgetting the cube root in radius ratios.
The most frequent slip is writing the radius ratio as the mass-number ratio. The correct relation is R proportional to A to the one third.
2. Believing heavier nuclei are denser.
Nuclear density is the same for every nucleus. If a question asks for a density ratio between two nuclei, the answer is 1 to 1 unless something other than A changes.
3. Mixing up isotopes, isobars and isotones.
Anchor each to its constant: isotopes hold Z, isobars hold A (bar = balance = same total weight), isotones hold N.
4. Confusing atomic mass with nuclear mass.
Tabulated masses usually include the Z electrons. When precision matters, be explicit about which mass you are using.
Pro-tip: memorise the perfect cubes 8, 27, 64, 125, 216. Examiners pick mass numbers near these so the cube root is instant.

segments.text: Let us close this subtopic by walking the four mistakes that actually appear in scripts. Every one of them is a place where a student who understood the physics still lost the mark.
Pitfall one, and it is the most frequent slip in the entire chapter. Forgetting the cube root when you take a radius ratio.

The temptation is obvious: the question gives you two mass numbers, so you divide them and write that down. But the correct relation is R proportional to A to the one third. Cube-root the mass-number ratio, always, before you write a single thing.
Pitfall two. Believing that heavier nuclei are denser. This feels so reasonable that students trust it over the derivation they wrote out ten minutes earlier.

Nuclear density is identical for every nucleus. So if a question asks for a density ratio between two nuclei, the answer is one to one, unless the question has changed something other than the mass number.
Pitfall three. Blurring the three families together, which is what the isotone question is designed to exploit.

The fix is to anchor each family to its constant. Isotopes hold the proton number Z. Isobars hold the mass number A, and think of bar as balance, as in same total weight. Isotones hold the neutron number N.
Pitfall four is subtler, and it will matter enormously in the next subtopic. Confusing atomic mass with nuclear mass.

Tabulated masses are usually atomic, meaning they quietly include the Z electrons as well as the nucleus. When precision matters, be explicit about whether you are using the proton mass, the neutron mass, or the neutral hydrogen atom mass.

<whisper>And one pro-tip to leave you with. Memorise the perfect cubes: two cubed is eight, three cubed is twenty seven, four cubed is sixty four, five cubed is one hundred and twenty five, six cubed is two hundred and sixteen. Examiners pick mass numbers near these on purpose, so recognising them turns a calculator problem into a mental one.
इस subtopic को उन चार गलतियों से बंद करते हैं जो सचमुच scripts में दिखती हैं। इनमें से हर एक वो जगह है जहाँ physics समझने वाला student भी mark गँवा देता है।
Pitfall one, और यह पूरे chapter की सबसे आम चूक है। Radius ratio लेते वक्त cube root भूल जाना।

लालच साफ़ है: question दो mass numbers देता है, तो आप भाग देकर लिख देते हैं। लेकिन सही relation है R proportional to A की power one third। कुछ भी लिखने से पहले mass number ratio का cube root लीजिए, हमेशा।
Pitfall two। यह मानना कि भारी nuclei ज़्यादा dense होते हैं। यह इतना reasonable लगता है कि students दस मिनट पहले लिखी अपनी derivation से ज़्यादा इस पर भरोसा कर लेते हैं।
Nuclear density हर nucleus के लिए एक जैसी है। तो अगर question दो nuclei के बीच density ratio माँगे, तो answer है one to one, जब तक question ने mass number के अलावा कुछ और न बदला हो।
Pitfall three। तीनों families को आपस में मिला देना, और isotone वाला question इसी को पकड़ने के लिए बनता है।
इलाज है हर family को उसके constant से बाँधना। Isotopes proton number Z पकड़ते हैं। Isobars mass number A, और bar को balance समझिए, यानी same total weight। Isotones neutron number N पकड़ते हैं।
Pitfall four ज़्यादा बारीक है, और अगले subtopic में यह बहुत मायने रखेगा। Atomic mass और nuclear mass को गड्डमड्ड कर देना।

Tabulated masses आम तौर पर atomic होते हैं, यानी उनमें nucleus के साथ Z electrons भी चुपचाप शामिल हैं। जहाँ precision ज़रूरी है, साफ़ लिखिए कि आप proton mass ले रहे हैं, neutron mass, या neutral hydrogen atom का mass।

<whisper>और आखिर में एक pro-tip। Perfect cubes याद कर लीजिए: दो का cube आठ, तीन का सत्ताईस, चार का चौंसठ, पाँच का एक सौ पच्चीस, छह का दो सौ सोलह। Examiners जानबूझकर इनके आसपास के mass numbers चुनते हैं, तो इन्हें पहचानना calculator वाले problem को दिमागी problem बना देता है।

board_events.text: An assembled nucleus weighs less than the loose protons and neutrons that make it up. That shortfall is the mass defect.
By $E = mc^2$, the missing mass did not vanish. It was released as energy when the nucleons snapped together.
Run the film backwards: the same energy must be supplied to tear the nucleus completely apart into free nucleons.
That energy is the binding energy $E_b$ of the nucleus.
Large binding energy = a deep well that is hard to climb out of = securely held together.
Binding energy is not something stored inside the nucleus. It is the energy that has already left.

segments.text: In the previous subtopic we met a strange fact and then walked past it rather quickly. Let us go back and take it seriously, because the whole of nuclear energy is hiding inside it.
Look at the two sides of the board. On the left, a bound nucleus. On the right, the same nucleons pulled apart and floating free. The arrows between them are the entire concept.
The fact was this. An assembled nucleus weighs less than the loose protons and neutrons that make it up. We called that shortfall the mass defect.
And Einstein told us where it went. That missing mass did not vanish. It was released as energy at the moment the nucleons snapped together into a nucleus.

<curious>Now here is the move that turns a curiosity into a physical quantity. Run the film backwards. If assembling the nucleus released a certain energy, then tearing it completely apart into free nucleons must cost exactly the same energy.
That energy has a name. It is the binding energy of the nucleus, written E sub b. It is the price of complete dismantling, and it is measured in mega electron volts.
So think of a nucleus as sitting at the bottom of a well. A nucleus with a large binding energy is in a deep well, hard to climb out of, and therefore deeply and securely held together.

One correction to a common picture before we go on. Binding energy is not something stored inside the nucleus, like fuel in a tank. It is the energy that has already left. That is precisely why the nucleus is lighter than its parts.
पिछले subtopic में हम एक अजीब fact से मिले थे और फिर जल्दी से आगे बढ़ गए। चलिए वापस चलते हैं और उसे गंभीरता से लेते हैं, क्योंकि पूरी nuclear energy उसी के अंदर छिपी है।
Board के दोनों तरफ देखिए। बाईं तरफ एक bound nucleus। दाईं तरफ वही nucleons अलग-अलग, खुले हुए। बीच के arrows ही पूरा concept हैं।
Fact यह था। तैयार nucleus उन loose protons और neutrons से हल्का होता है जिनसे वो बना है। इसी कमी को हमने mass defect कहा था।
और Einstein ने बताया वो कहाँ गया। वो गायब mass खत्म नहीं हुआ। वो उसी पल energy बनकर निकल गया जब nucleons आपस में जुड़कर nucleus बने।

<curious>अब वो move जो एक जिज्ञासा को physical quantity बना देता है। Film को उल्टा चलाइए। अगर nucleus बनने पर कोई energy निकली थी, तो उसे पूरी तरह तोड़कर free nucleons बनाने में ठीक उतनी ही energy लगेगी।
इस energy का नाम है। यही है nucleus की binding energy, लिखते हैं E sub b। यह पूरी तरह तोड़ने की कीमत है, और इसे mega electron volts में नापते हैं।
तो nucleus को सोचिए एक कुएँ की तली में बैठा हुआ। बड़ी binding energy वाला nucleus गहरे कुएँ में है, जहाँ से निकलना मुश्किल है, यानी वो मज़बूती से बँधा हुआ है।
आगे बढ़ने से पहले एक आम गलतफ़हमी सुधार लेते हैं। Binding energy nucleus के अंदर जमा नहीं है, जैसे tank में fuel। यह वो energy है जो पहले ही जा चुकी है। और ठीक इसीलिए nucleus अपने parts से हल्का है।

board_events.text: To compare stability fairly, divide by the number of nucleons and ask: how much glue does each nucleon get?
Cricket analogy: judge two teams by their batting average, runs per player, not by total runs.
Binding energy per nucleon is the single most important quantity in nuclear physics.
Higher $E_b/A$ means a more stable nucleus. It measures how tightly the typical nucleon is held, independent of how big the nucleus is.

segments.text: We now have a number for how tightly a nucleus is held. The obvious next step is to use it to rank nuclei by stability. And if you do that naively, you get the wrong answer.

Here is why. A uranium nucleus has a far larger total binding energy than a helium nucleus. But that is not because uranium is better bound. It is simply because uranium has many more nucleons to bind in the first place.
Look at the comparison. On the left, judged by total binding energy, uranium towers over helium. On the right, judged the fairer way, the two are almost level.
So to compare stability honestly we divide by the number of nucleons and ask a better question. Not how much glue is there in total, but how much glue does each individual nucleon get?
That quantity is the binding energy per nucleon, E sub b divided by A, which is the mass defect times c squared, all over the mass number.

The analogy the chapter gives is a good one. You do not judge two cricket teams by their total runs, because one team may simply have batted more. You judge them by the batting average, runs per player.

<excited>And this is not just a tidier way of presenting the same information. Binding energy per nucleon is the single most important quantity in all of nuclear physics. Almost every remaining result in this chapter is a statement about it.

The rule to carry forward is simple. Higher binding energy per nucleon means a more stable nucleus. It is a stability average, telling you how tightly the typical nucleon is held, and deliberately independent of how big the nucleus happens to be.
अब हमारे पास एक number है कि nucleus कितनी मज़बूती से बँधा है। अगला कदम साफ़ है, इससे nuclei को stability के हिसाब से रैंक करना। और अगर आप यह सीधे-सीधे करेंगे, तो जवाब गलत आएगा।
वजह यह है। Uranium nucleus की total binding energy helium से कहीं ज़्यादा है। पर इसलिए नहीं कि uranium बेहतर bound है। सिर्फ इसलिए कि uranium में बाँधने के लिए nucleons ही कहीं ज़्यादा हैं।
Comparison देखिए। बाईं तरफ, total binding energy से आँकें तो uranium helium पर भारी पड़ता है। दाईं तरफ, ज़्यादा सही तरीके से आँकें तो दोनों लगभग बराबर हैं।
तो ईमानदारी से compare करने के लिए हम nucleons की संख्या से भाग देते हैं और बेहतर सवाल पूछते हैं। कुल कितना glue है यह नहीं, बल्कि हर एक nucleon को कितना glue मिला।
यही quantity है binding energy per nucleon, E sub b बटा A, यानी mass defect into c squared, पूरे का mass number से भाग।
Chapter जो analogy देता है वो बढ़िया है। आप दो cricket teams को total runs से नहीं आँकते, क्योंकि हो सकता है एक team ने ज़्यादा batting की हो। आप batting average से आँकते हैं, यानी runs per player।

<excited>और यह सिर्फ वही जानकारी सलीके से दिखाने का तरीका नहीं है। Binding energy per nucleon पूरी nuclear physics की सबसे अहम quantity है। इस chapter का लगभग हर बचा हुआ result इसी के बारे में एक statement है।

आगे ले जाने वाला rule आसान है। ज़्यादा binding energy per nucleon यानी ज़्यादा stable nucleus। यह एक stability average है, जो बताता है कि आम nucleon कितनी मज़बूती से पकड़ा हुआ है, और जानबूझकर इस बात से बेपरवाह है कि nucleus कितना बड़ा है।

board_events.text: Starting from light nuclei, the curve climbs steeply.
It reaches a broad peak of about 8.8 MeV per nucleon near A = 56, the iron and nickel region.
It then declines gently, dropping to about 7.6 MeV per nucleon by the time we reach uranium.
Iron-region nuclei are the most tightly bound and most stable. Every other nucleus would 'prefer' to move toward that peak.
Light nuclei can climb toward the peak by joining together: fusion.
Heavy nuclei can climb toward the peak by splitting apart: fission. In both cases the products are more tightly bound, so the surplus is released.
Limits: this is a smooth average trend. Nuclei with magic numbers of protons or neutrons (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) are unusually stable; helium-4 sits noticeably above its neighbours.

segments.text: Everything so far has been preparation for this one graph. If you take a single image away from this chapter, make it this one, because it explains reactors, stars and the periodic table's upper limit all at once.

We plot binding energy per nucleon on the vertical axis against mass number on the horizontal axis, for every nucleus we know. And what emerges is not a scatter of random points. It is a beautifully revealing curve.

Read it left to right. Starting from the lightest nuclei, the curve climbs steeply. The deuteron sits right down at the bottom left, barely bound at all, and within a few nucleons we are already most of the way up.

The climb then flattens into a broad peak of about eight point eight mega electron volts per nucleon, near mass number fifty six. That is the iron and nickel region, and it is the summit of the entire graph.
After the peak, the curve declines, but gently. By the time we reach uranium at mass number two hundred and thirty eight, it has drifted down to about seven point six mega electron volts per nucleon.
Now read the message rather than the shape. Iron-region nuclei are the most tightly bound and the most stable nuclei in existence, and every other nucleus would prefer to move toward that peak.
So look at the two arrows. On the rising left-hand side, a light nucleus can climb toward the peak by joining with another one. That is fusion.

<excited>And on the falling right-hand side, a heavy nucleus can climb toward that same peak by splitting apart. That is fission. In both cases the products end up more tightly bound than what you started with, so the surplus binding energy comes out as released energy. Two opposite processes, one explanation.

One honest limitation. This curve is a smooth average trend, and real nuclei show small bumps around it. Nuclei with so-called magic numbers of protons or neutrons, that is two, eight, twenty, twenty eight, fifty, eighty two and one hundred and twenty six, are unusually stable. Helium-four is the visible example, sitting noticeably above its neighbours.
अब तक सब कुछ इसी एक graph की तैयारी था। अगर इस chapter से आप एक ही image ले जा सकें, तो यही ले जाइए, क्योंकि यह reactors, stars और periodic table की ऊपरी सीमा, तीनों एक साथ समझा देता है।

हम vertical axis पर binding energy per nucleon और horizontal axis पर mass number लेते हैं, हर जाने-पहचाने nucleus के लिए। और जो उभरता है वो बिखरे हुए points नहीं हैं। वो एक बेहद खुलासा करने वाली curve है।
बाएँ से दाएँ पढ़िए। सबसे हल्के nuclei से शुरू होकर curve तेज़ी से चढ़ती है। Deuteron बिल्कुल नीचे बाईं तरफ बैठा है, मुश्किल से bound, और कुछ ही nucleons में हम लगभग ऊपर पहुँच जाते हैं।
फिर चढ़ाई चौड़े peak में बदल जाती है, लगभग आठ point आठ mega electron volts per nucleon, mass number छप्पन के आसपास। यही iron और nickel का इलाका है, और यही पूरे graph की चोटी है।
Peak के बाद curve गिरती है, पर धीरे-धीरे। जब तक हम mass number दो सौ अड़तीस पर uranium तक पहुँचते हैं, यह खिसककर लगभग seven point six mega electron volts per nucleon रह जाती है।
अब shape नहीं, message पढ़िए। Iron वाले इलाके के nuclei मौजूद सभी nuclei में सबसे मज़बूती से bound और सबसे stable हैं, और बाकी हर nucleus उसी peak की तरफ जाना चाहेगा।
तो दोनों arrows देखिए। चढ़ती हुई बाईं तरफ, एक हल्का nucleus दूसरे से जुड़कर peak की तरफ चढ़ सकता है। यही है fusion।

<excited>और गिरती हुई दाईं तरफ, एक भारी nucleus टूटकर उसी peak की तरफ चढ़ सकता है। यही है fission। दोनों ही हालात में products शुरुआती material से ज़्यादा मज़बूती से bound निकलते हैं, तो बची हुई binding energy बाहर आ जाती है। दो उल्टे processes, एक ही explanation।

एक ईमानदार limitation। यह curve एक smooth average trend है, और असली nuclei इसके आसपास छोटे उभार दिखाते हैं। जिन nuclei में protons या neutrons की तथाकथित magic numbers होती हैं, यानी दो, आठ, बीस, अट्ठाईस, पचास, बयासी और एक सौ छब्बीस, वो असामान्य रूप से stable होते हैं। Helium-four इसका दिखने वाला example है, जो अपने पड़ोसियों से साफ़ ऊपर बैठा है।

board_events.text: Steep rise, light nuclei: in a tiny nucleus most nucleons sit on the surface, with few neighbours to bond to.
Add nucleons and each new one finds more partners, so $E_b/A$ climbs quickly. This is the volume-versus-surface competition: surface nucleons are under-bonded.
Broad peak near A = 56: here the short-range force is saturated.
Adding more nucleons no longer increases the binding per nucleon, because a nucleon only ever feels its nearest neighbours. Stability is maximised.
Gentle fall, heavy nuclei: every proton repels every other proton through the long-range Coulomb force.
Disruptive electrostatic energy grows like $Z^2$, faster than attractive binding can keep up, so the typical nucleon is held slightly less tightly.

segments.text: A curve is only worth memorising if you know why it bends the way it does. So let us take the three regions in turn, because each one has a completely different physical mechanism behind it.
Here they are side by side. Notice that the picture in each panel is about neighbours. How many partners does a typical nucleon have to bond with? That single question drives all three regions.
Region one, the steep rise on the left. In a tiny nucleus, almost every nucleon is sitting on the surface, exposed, with very few neighbours around it to bond to.

So when you add another nucleon, everybody suddenly has more partners, and the binding per nucleon climbs quickly. This is the volume-versus-surface competition, and the short version is that surface nucleons are under-bonded.
Region two, the broad peak near mass number fifty six. Something changes here, and the word for it is saturation.

Remember that the nuclear force is short-range. A nucleon only ever feels its nearest neighbours, never the whole nucleus. So once a nucleon is fully surrounded, adding more nucleons somewhere else does nothing for it. The binding per nucleon stops rising, and stability is at its maximum.
Region three, the gentle fall on the right. And here a completely different force takes over the story: the electric one.

<whisper>Because the Coulomb force is long-range. Every proton repels every other proton, right across the nucleus, so the disruptive electrostatic energy grows like Z squared. That grows faster than the attractive binding can keep up with, so the typical nucleon ends up slightly less tightly held, and the curve slowly slides down.
Curve तभी याद रखने लायक है जब आपको पता हो वो ऐसे मुड़ती क्यों है। तो चलिए तीनों regions एक-एक करके लेते हैं, क्योंकि हर एक के पीछे बिल्कुल अलग physical mechanism है।
यह रहे तीनों साथ-साथ। ध्यान दीजिए हर panel की तस्वीर पड़ोसियों के बारे में है। एक आम nucleon के पास bond बनाने के लिए कितने partners हैं? यही एक सवाल तीनों regions चलाता है।
Region one, बाईं तरफ की तेज़ चढ़ाई। छोटे nucleus में लगभग हर nucleon surface पर बैठा है, खुला हुआ, और उसके आसपास bond बनाने के लिए बहुत कम पड़ोसी हैं।

तो जब आप एक और nucleon जोड़ते हैं, अचानक सबको ज़्यादा partners मिल जाते हैं, और binding per nucleon तेज़ी से चढ़ती है। यही है volume बनाम surface की होड़, और छोटा जवाब यह है कि surface वाले nucleons under-bonded होते हैं।
Region two, mass number छप्पन के पास चौड़ा peak। यहाँ कुछ बदलता है, और उसका नाम है saturation।

याद रखिए nuclear force short-range है। एक nucleon सिर्फ अपने सबसे पास वाले पड़ोसियों को महसूस करता है, पूरे nucleus को कभी नहीं। तो एक बार nucleon पूरी तरह घिर गया, तो कहीं और nucleons जोड़ने से उसे कुछ नहीं मिलता। Binding per nucleon बढ़ना बंद, और stability अपने अधिकतम पर।
Region three, दाईं तरफ की हल्की ढलान। और यहाँ कहानी एक बिल्कुल अलग force संभाल लेती है: electric force।

<whisper>क्योंकि Coulomb force long-range है। हर proton हर दूसरे proton को धकेलता है, पूरे nucleus के आर-पार, तो तोड़ने वाली electrostatic energy Z squared की तरह बढ़ती है। यह attractive binding के साथ चलने की रफ़्तार से तेज़ बढ़ती है, तो आम nucleon थोड़ा कम कसकर पकड़ा जाता है, और curve धीरे-धीरे नीचे खिसकती है।

sections.title: The strong nuclear force and the shape of its potential

board_events.text: What actually supplies all that binding?
Not gravity: far too weak at this scale. Not the electric force: it only pushes the protons apart.
A distinct, powerful interaction, the strong nuclear force, overpowers electrostatic repulsion and clamps the nucleons together.

board_events.text: Below about 0.7 fm the force turns strongly repulsive. This prevents the nucleus from collapsing and fixes the inter-nucleon spacing.
Around 1 fm sits a deep attractive well, of order minus 50 MeV. This is where the binding comes from.
By 2 to 3 fm the potential has returned to essentially zero. The force is short-range and simply switches off.
About 100 times the electrostatic force at nuclear separations: the strongest of the basic forces in its own domain.
It is also charge-independent: the nuclear attraction between neutron-neutron, neutron-proton and proton-proton pairs is the same. It does not care about electric charge.

segments.text: <curious>We have been talking about binding energy for a while now without ever asking the obvious question. What is actually doing the binding? What force is strong enough to hold ninety two mutually repelling protons in a ball a few femtometres across?

Let us eliminate the candidates you already know. Gravity is far too weak at this scale, by something like thirty six orders of magnitude. And the electric force is worse than useless here, because between protons it pushes outward, actively trying to blow the nucleus apart.
So there must be something else, and there is. A distinct and powerful interaction, the strong nuclear force, which overpowers the electrostatic repulsion and clamps the nucleons together.
The cleanest way to understand it is to plot the potential energy between two nucleons against their separation. Everything about the force is visible in the shape of this one curve.

Start at the left, at very small separations. Below about zero point seven femtometres the curve shoots upward, which means the force has turned strongly repulsive. That repulsive core is what stops the nucleus collapsing in on itself, and it fixes the spacing between nucleons.

Move right and the curve plunges into a deep attractive well, around one femtometre, of order minus fifty mega electron volts. This well is where all the binding comes from. This is the region a nucleon actually lives in.

Keep going right and something striking happens. By two to three femtometres the curve has come back to essentially zero and stays there. The force does not fade away gradually like gravity. It simply switches off.

For scale, at nuclear separations this force is about a hundred times stronger than the electrostatic force. Within its own domain it is the strongest of the basic forces, which is exactly why it wins against Coulomb repulsion.

<whisper>And one property that surprises students. The strong force is charge-independent. The nuclear attraction between two neutrons, between a neutron and a proton, and between two protons is the same. It does not care about electric charge at all.

<curious>हम काफी देर से binding energy की बात कर रहे हैं और वो सीधा सवाल पूछा ही नहीं। असल में binding कर कौन रहा है? कौन सी force इतनी ताकतवर है कि बानवे आपस में धकेलते protons को कुछ femtometre की गेंद में रोक ले?

जो forces आप पहले से जानते हैं, उन्हें हटा देते हैं। इस scale पर gravity बहुत ही कमज़ोर है, लगभग छत्तीस orders of magnitude से। और electric force तो यहाँ बेकार से भी बदतर है, क्योंकि protons के बीच वो बाहर की तरफ धकेलती है, nucleus को तोड़ने की कोशिश करती हुई।
तो कुछ और होना चाहिए, और है। एक अलग, ताकतवर interaction, strong nuclear force, जो electrostatic repulsion पर भारी पड़ती है और nucleons को जकड़कर रखती है।
इसे समझने का सबसे साफ़ तरीका है दो nucleons के बीच potential energy को उनकी separation के against plot करना। इस एक curve की shape में force के बारे में सब कुछ दिख जाता है।

बाईं तरफ से शुरू कीजिए, बहुत छोटी separations पर। लगभग zero point seven femtometre से नीचे curve ऊपर की तरफ भागती है, यानी force strongly repulsive हो गई है। यही repulsive core nucleus को अपने अंदर ढहने से रोकता है, और nucleons के बीच की दूरी तय करता है।

दाईं तरफ बढ़िए और curve एक गहरे attractive well में गोता लगाती है, लगभग एक femtometre पर, करीब minus पचास mega electron volts का। सारी binding इसी well से आती है। असल में nucleon इसी इलाके में रहता है।
और दाईं तरफ चलिए तो एक चौंकाने वाली बात होती है। दो से तीन femtometre तक curve वापस लगभग zero पर आ जाती है और वहीं रहती है। यह force gravity की तरह धीरे-धीरे कम नहीं होती। यह बस बंद हो जाती है।
Scale समझिए, nuclear separations पर यह force electrostatic force से लगभग सौ गुना ताकतवर है। अपने इलाके में यह basic forces में सबसे ताकतवर है, और इसीलिए यह Coulomb repulsion से जीत जाती है।

<whisper>और एक property जो students को चौंकाती है। Strong force charge-independent है। दो neutrons के बीच, एक neutron और एक proton के बीच, और दो protons के बीच nuclear attraction एक जैसी है। उसे electric charge की परवाह ही नहीं।

<text x="350" y="256" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" text-anchor="middle" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">Extra neutrons add binding without adding charge, which is exactly</text>
<text x="350" y="274" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#22303c" text-anchor="middle" paint-order="stroke fill" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2px">what a proton-rich heavy nucleus needs against Coulomb repulsion.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Light stable nuclei have roughly equal numbers of protons and neutrons: N is about equal to Z.
As nuclei grow heavier, the Coulomb repulsion between protons demands extra neutrons.
Extra neutrons add binding without adding charge, which is exactly what a proton-rich nucleus needs.
So the stable ratio drifts upward to about $N/Z = 1.5$ for the heaviest stable nuclei.
Step too far from this stability band and the nucleus becomes radioactive. That is the bridge into the next subtopic.
This one graph explains why heavy elements are neutron-rich, and why the periodic table eventually runs out of stable nuclei altogether.

segments.text: We know a nucleus needs neutrons, because a nucleus of pure protons would blow itself apart. The sharper question is how many, and the answer changes as nuclei get heavier.
Plot every stable nucleus with neutron number up the side and proton number along the bottom, and the stable ones do not scatter randomly. They fall along a narrow band.

Down at the light end, that band sits almost exactly on the dashed line where N equals Z. Light stable nuclei carry roughly equal numbers of protons and neutrons. Carbon-twelve has six of each; oxygen-sixteen has eight of each.

But as nuclei grow heavier, the band peels away from that line and rises above it. The reason is Coulomb repulsion. Every additional proton repels every other proton, and that disruptive energy is growing fast.

So the nucleus needs reinforcement, and neutrons are the perfect reinforcement. A neutron contributes to the strong-force binding but carries no charge, so it adds glue without adding any extra repulsion.

The result is a steady drift in the ratio. From about one to one for light nuclei, it climbs to roughly one point five neutrons per proton for the heaviest stable nuclei. Lead and bismuth sit right at the top of that band.

<curious>And now the question that opens the next subtopic. What happens if a nucleus sits off the band, with too many neutrons or too few? The answer is that it does not stay there. It becomes radioactive, and it rearranges itself until it reaches the band.

So this single graph is doing a lot of work. It explains why heavy elements are neutron-rich, why the ratio drifts rather than staying fixed, and ultimately why the periodic table runs out of stable nuclei altogether once the band can no longer be reached.
हमें पता है कि nucleus को neutrons चाहिए, क्योंकि सिर्फ protons वाला nucleus खुद को उड़ा देगा। असली सवाल है कितने, और यह जवाब nuclei के भारी होने के साथ बदलता है।
हर stable nucleus को plot कीजिए, ऊपर की तरफ neutron number और नीचे की तरफ proton number, तो stable वाले बेतरतीब नहीं बिखरते। वो एक पतली band में गिरते हैं।
हल्के सिरे पर वो band लगभग ठीक उसी dashed line पर बैठी है जहाँ N बराबर Z है। हल्के stable nuclei में protons और neutrons लगभग बराबर होते हैं। Carbon-twelve में छह-छह; oxygen-sixteen में आठ-आठ।
लेकिन जैसे-जैसे nuclei भारी होते हैं, band उस line से हटकर ऊपर उठ जाती है। वजह है Coulomb repulsion। हर नया proton हर दूसरे proton को धकेलता है, और वो तोड़ने वाली energy तेज़ी से बढ़ रही है।
तो nucleus को मज़बूती चाहिए, और neutrons उसके लिए एकदम सही हैं। Neutron strong-force binding में हिस्सा डालता है पर कोई charge नहीं लाता, यानी glue जुड़ता है और repulsion बिल्कुल नहीं बढ़ता।

नतीजा है ratio का लगातार खिसकना। हल्के nuclei के लिए लगभग one to one से, यह सबसे भारी stable nuclei के लिए करीब one point five neutrons per proton तक चढ़ जाता है। Lead और bismuth उसी band के सबसे ऊपरी सिरे पर बैठे हैं।

<curious>और अब वो सवाल जो अगला subtopic खोलता है। अगर कोई nucleus band से हटकर बैठा हो, बहुत ज़्यादा neutrons या बहुत कम, तो क्या होगा? जवाब यह है कि वो वहाँ टिकता नहीं। वो radioactive हो जाता है, और खुद को तब तक बदलता है जब तक band तक न पहुँच जाए।

तो यह अकेला graph बहुत काम कर रहा है। यह बताता है कि भारी elements neutron-rich क्यों होते हैं, ratio fixed रहने के बजाय खिसकता क्यों है, और आखिरकार periodic table में stable nuclei खत्म क्यों हो जाते हैं, जब band तक पहुँचना ही नामुमकिन हो जाता है।

board_events.text: Binding energy: the working formulas
Using neutral-atom masses instead, the electron masses cancel automatically:
Unit of the mass defect: u. Dimensional formula $[M^1 L^0 T^0]$. It is always positive.
